title: Chapter 18.3 Suggestion for additional note to explain concept
description:
In **internal functions**.

There's example code with separate shiny internal function. 

before
``` r
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  switch_page <- function(i) {
    updateTabsetPanel(input = "wizard", selected = paste0("page_", i))
  }
  
  observeEvent(input$page_12, switch_page(2))
  observeEvent(input$page_21, switch_page(1))
  observeEvent(input$page_23, switch_page(3))
  observeEvent(input$page_32, switch_page(2))
}
```

after
``` r
switch_page <- function(i) {
  updateTabsetPanel(input = "wizard", selected = paste0("page_", i))
}

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  observeEvent(input$page_12, switch_page(2))
  observeEvent(input$page_21, switch_page(1))
  observeEvent(input$page_23, switch_page(3))
  observeEvent(input$page_32, switch_page(2))
}
```

Changed: `switch_page` function "moved out" of `server` function. 

And there's explanation like below
> "We could of course add `session` to the arguments of the function:"

However, the code is not much different as explained. (`session` is not mentioned in code)
Since shiny's updated version (`updateTabesetPanel()`) use `session` with `getDefaultReactiveDomain()` as default parameter. 

So I suggest to mention like below and why session parameter didn't used to avoid confusion.

---

We could of course add `session` to the arguments of the function:

``` r
switch_page <- function(session, i){
  updateTabsetPanel(session, input = "wizard", selected = paste0("page_", i))
}

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  observeEvent(input$page_12, switch_page(session, 2))
  observeEvent(input$page_21, switch_page(session, 1))
  observeEvent(input$page_23, switch_page(session, 3))
  observeEvent(input$page_32, switch_page(session, 2))
}
```

However, since shiny > 1.6 uses update- function (like updateTabsetPanel) uses `session` as default pameter, 
we can skip the `session` like below

``` r
switch_page <- function(i) {
  updateTabsetPanel(input = "wizard", selected = paste0("page_", i))
}

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  observeEvent(input$page_12, switch_page(2))
  observeEvent(input$page_21, switch_page(1))
  observeEvent(input$page_23, switch_page(3))
  observeEvent(input$page_32, switch_page(2))
}
```

But this feels weird as the function is still fundamentally coupled to this app because it only affects a control named “wizard” with a very specific set of tabs.

---


Thanks.

title: Needs database and async coverage
description:
Very good book, Hadley! Say, I'm running into issues with using Shiny to display very large data (data sets running up to hundreds of thousands of rows). I've been looking for resources online which could help address strategies for handling big data, particularly when we're querying data stores like Snowflake. Clearly the most obvious strategies are filtering, limiting, and sampling, but what about after you've done all of that, and now you're trying to figure out how to build the most performant Shiny app possible. Strategies like async/futures might help (if the same large data set is used in other areas of the app, e.g., on other tabs maybe lazy load it?), maybe strategies like chunking data loading from Snowflake (at least where you don't need all the data all at once), or maybe strategies for how you can cache a default data set (which is smaller and therefore will load faster), but then load live data from the DB when a different option is selected in a dropdown. 

Anyway, I have yet to see any kind of robust coverage of how to handle large to huge data with R/Shiny--and just generally how to make performant Shiny apps. I'd love it if you'd add more on this to your book. Thanks for your consideration!

library(shinytest)

ui <- fluidPage(
  numericInput("x", "x", value = 3, min = 1, max = 5),

title: More guidance on deployment
description:
This book is wonderful and has been extremely valuable in creating Shiny apps. Thank you!

I know the book specifically says that it will not cover deployment, but I am wondering if could cover it at least a little bit. Like all of your other books, this one is very well written for a specific audience. The deployment links included in the preface lead to resources not written for the same audience. I think it would be easy to cruise through this book believing "A Shiny app can support thousands or tens of thousands of users, if developed the right way." (Ch 23) and not realize there is also a huge IF you can find the proper IT support. 

Somewhere it needs to be laid out: If you want your app to run well on the world wide web, you need to find a real life person willing to set up and maintain a real life server. You are going to have to work outside the online R community (possibly for the first time). You need to take a convincing Shiny Server or RStudio Connect pitch to this server-person. Or you need to take a convincing pitch to this person's manager. Or you need to learn to run your own server. 

Assuming the people reading this book have not made an app before, they have also not had the need for any infrastructure to support an app. I think the first time I made a Shiny app was the first time I learned what a server is. If this book is going to be the authoritative resource for Shiny beginners, I think it needs a little bit more on what to do when the coding is done. I'd be happy to help. 

(And I realize that shinyapps.io is an easy option for deployment, but there are a lot of reasons I don't believe it is a good option. As far as I can tell, it is one of RStudio's lowest priorities.)

title: Suggestions on examples
description:
I've been writing Shiny apps in recent 2 years and learned a lot from scattered places. It will be great to have one book to include all the key ideas.

In my learning experience, I think some good examples can really help readers to understand the concept and apply to their own problems. I also would like to share some of tricks I think are very useful.

My first suggestion of example is based on my two answers in Stackoverflow - 
[Add weblink to actionButton](https://stackoverflow.com/a/42819294/3718827), basically I used actionButton css class for a link, so a link will look like a button. Further more we can make a [material button for a link](https://stackoverflow.com/a/44073698/3718827). The key take away in this example is to print the tag function output, explore and set attributes properly. 

In customizing css part, it's also worth mentioning the development tools within rstudio or chrome which can work on shiny app directly(you probably have this in mind already).

In reactivity part:
- turning on `options(shiny.trace = TRUE)` is often very helpful(I found the reactive log is often overwhelming and less useful).
- data.table modify variable by reference, so if user was using a data.table for reactive value, they need to set it to NULL then update value again to trigger reactive changes.
- req is very useful to prevent unwanted error messages or behaviors. However req cannot be used inside data.table bracket like dt[req(var), .N], probably because when req returned Error it was not handled properly inside data.table. req has to be used outside of data.table call.
- if the execution order of multiple reactive parts is not working as expected,`freezeReactiveValue` can be helpful (I found different priority settings never worked for me), but often there is a better design by choosing different reactive variables.

I also have to go through lots of trial and errors in using DT row selection to trigger app behavior, because the row selection event was the slowest in shiny app, which often create problem of updates order in reactive context. I can help to provide some example on this but not sure if there is a need for this kind of usage.

title: Staging and production
description:
https://rstudio.com/resources/rstudioconf-2019/shiny-in-production-principles-practices-and-tools/

* Production environment = real app used by real people. If it breaks, people will complain. Environment = everything. Not just your app, but the server that it runs on, database it connects to, ... Includes anything that can affect your app.

* Staging environment = best practice. Set up a clone of your prod env. So you can do a dress rehearsal. Also have your development machine, but that's likely to be more different — might have local copy of data, might be your mac laptop vs linux server, ...

What is production:

* Keep it up
* Keep it safe 
* Keep it correct
* Keep it snappy

Challenges:

* Cultural: most R users don't have a software engineering background. Might not know what best practices are. Might not have budgeted time needed for best practices. Might take just as long as developing initial app! And generally, don't prioritise run-time efficiency (tend to care more about expressive APIs, rapid explorationg)
* Organisational: IT/management sceptical (naturally conservative; sceptical about data scientists deploying to production; sceptical about technology they haven't heard of). Software engineer org might not be on your side (have heard that "R is not a real language")
* Technical: shiny makes it much easier to make an app. But it hasn't made it easier to handle other parts of making a production app.

title: Is the book license ShareAlike or NoDerivatives?
description:
The intro says that the book is licensed under [CC BY-NC-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/) (*ShareAlike*):

https://github.com/hadley/mastering-shiny/blob/066b8c035c3ebed16983f6c8cdbdbd16656729d8/index.Rmd#L31

But the README says that the book is licensed under [CC BY-NC-ND 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/) (*NoDerivatives*), which is more restrictive:

https://github.com/hadley/mastering-shiny/blob/066b8c035c3ebed16983f6c8cdbdbd16656729d8/README.md#L5

I am asking because I have been working through the exercises of the book in my own fork, which I built and deployed via Netlify ([here](https://mastering-shiny-mpc-solutions.netlify.com/basic-app.html#exercises)). As I understand it, what I am doing is OK under a ShareAlike license but would violate a NoDerivatives license because: 

> If you remix, transform, or build upon the material, you may not distribute the modified material.

Anyways, I really don't mind taking down my deployed site (I can still build my version locally), but I thought I should flag the license inconsistencies in case it might become an issue!
